summary: Gives concrete recommendations and a unified method for getting SIP and its media sessions through NATs, and documents the corresponding message flows. NAT traversal is complex because of the many deployment scenarios and mechanisms. It is informational guidance for client-server SIP.

plainLanguage.summary: Phone calls over the internet have trouble crossing the doors that home routers put up. This explains one recommended set of tricks to get calls through and shows how the messages flow.

subtitle: Getting phone calls through NAT barriers: unified practices and message flows

tldr.problem: Voice calls over the Internet using SIP fail when traversing Network Address Translators because responses and media cannot find their way back through private networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC consolidates existing IETF technologies (symmetric response, ICE, STUN, TURN) into unified best practices for both SIP signaling and real-time audio/video media, with detailed message flows for common deployment scenarios.
tldr.outcome: Provides concrete, tested guidance that practitioners can follow to deploy SIP successfully across NAT boundaries without proprietary workarounds.

facts.label: Core issue
facts.value: Responses sent to wrong port, inbound requests blocked

facts.label: Scenario count
facts.value: Multiple registration, session initiation, and media traversal flows

today: RFC 6314 is an Informational RFC published in July 2011. The techniques it documents are now standard in SIP deployments: ICE is the recommended approach for media traversal, and SIP Outbound is widely implemented for signaling. The combination of symmetric response, connection reuse, STUN, TURN, and ICE remains the mainstream solution for SIP across NATs.

sections.title: The NAT Traversal Problem
sections.content:
Network Address Translators (NATs) are ubiquitous in deployment: home routers, corporate firewalls, and mobile networks all use NATs to map private IP addresses to public ones. This creates a fundamental problem for voice calls using SIP: responses cannot route back correctly, inbound calls cannot reach private devices, and media packets cannot travel bidirectionally.

The Internet Engineering Task Force has produced many partial solutions (STUN, TURN, ICE, symmetric response, various SIP extensions), but each addresses only one part of the problem. This RFC serves as a unified best-practices guide, showing how to combine these technologies and documenting the actual message flows that result, so that implementers and deployers can reference concrete examples.
sections.plainLanguage: Your home router stops incoming calls automatically. People invented several ways to fix this, but nobody explained how they fit together. This document shows which tricks work, in what order, with real examples.

sections.title: Where SIP and Media Fail
sections.content:
SIP signaling has multiple failure modes behind NATs. When a client sends a SIP REGISTER or INVITE request through a NAT, it creates a temporary opening (a pinhole) for the NAT to forward responses back. But the SIP header specifies the port the response should use, which is the internal listening port, not the NAT's pinhole. The response arrives at the wrong port and is dropped. Additionally, inbound requests destined to the private address cannot be routed because only the outbound direction has an active mapping.

Media traversal is equally complex: RTP/RTCP runs over UDP and travels on address/port pairs advertised via SDP in the SIP signaling. When these addresses are private, external parties cannot reach them. Different NAT types (endpoint-independent, address-dependent, port-dependent) behave differently, requiring different solutions. RTCP also violates the assumption that it will arrive on a port adjacent to RTP, breaking many NAT implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Responses go to the wrong port and disappear. Incoming calls hit a wall. Audio endpoints advertise private addresses nobody can reach. Different routers handle this differently, making one solution not work for everyone.

sections.title: The Best-Practice Toolkit
sections.content:
For SIP signaling, the document recommends two complementary practices. Symmetric response (RFC 3581) instructs the proxy to send responses back through the same IP and port the request originated from, rather than the SIP header's advertised port. The client includes an 'rport' parameter in its Via header to enable this. Second, SIP Outbound (RFC 5626) provides a mechanism for clients to maintain long-lived connections to proxies and reuse them for inbound requests. The proxy stores a flow identifier (a unique token associated with the client's connection) and routes inbound requests to that connection, bypassing the need for the client to accept inbound connections.

For media traversal, the RFC recommends combining multiple technologies. Symmetric RTP/RTCP (RFC 4961) means sending and receiving media from the same port, which works with NAT latching (a common NAT behavior). STUN (RFC 5389) discovers the public IP/port the NAT assigns to a private address. TURN (RFC 5766) provides a relay server when direct paths fail. ICE (RFC 5245) is the recommended comprehensive solution: it gathers candidate addresses using STUN/TURN, includes them in SDP, and runs connectivity checks to find which pair works.
sections.plainLanguage: For voice calls: use connection reuse and poke holes from the inside. For audio: learn your public address, try all paths, use a relay as a fallback. ICE tries everything and picks what works.

sections.title: Real Message Flows and Scenarios
sections.content:
The bulk of the RFC consists of detailed message flow diagrams and actual SIP/SDP examples showing how these techniques work in practice. Scenarios include REGISTER flows using both UDP and connection-oriented transport (TCP), with and without co-located registrars and proxies. Each example includes the exact SIP message content, highlighting the critical headers: 'rport' and 'received' parameters in Via headers, 'reg-id' and 'sip.instance' contact parameters for outbound binding, and Path headers for edge proxy insertion.

Media traversal scenarios show STUN binding discovery for endpoint-independent NATs, where a client queries a STUN server to learn its external address and includes that in SDP. They also cover ICE, which accumulates multiple candidate addresses with priority rankings and runs checks to establish connectivity. Address-dependent and port-dependent NAT scenarios are included, showing when STUN fails and TURN becomes necessary. All diagrams use consistent notation and identify the specific addresses and ports at each step.
sections.plainLanguage: Complete step-by-step examples show what each message looks like, what the router does at each stage, and how the call actually gets through. Different router types are covered: some need special tricks, others need a relay.

sections.title: Security and IPv4-IPv6 Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that it assumes NATs without SIP-aware Application Layer Gateways (ALGs), which often interfere with SIP more than they help. A section addresses IPv4 to IPv6 transition for SIP signaling, acknowledging that multihomed hosts may have both protocol versions available and SIP clients must handle mixed scenarios.

Security is treated in summary form: the RFC focuses on the traversal mechanisms and notes that operators must secure their STUN and TURN infrastructure, and that SIP Outbound client certificates and return-routability checks provide identity assurance. The goal is to provide concrete guidance without duplicating security analysis from underlying protocol specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Watch out for router firmware that tries to be too smart about SIP. Hosts with both IPv4 and IPv6 need both to work. Relays must be trusted.
